1. **The idea:** The frames show whether buying a home beat renting over ten-year periods in US history. Each cell in the grid seems to be one starting month between January 1991 and July 2016. A lit cell means the buyer was ahead after ten years, and a dark cell means the renter was ahead. The labels cite FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The grid is marked "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. **What changes over time:** Not much changes across the six frames. The grid is almost the same in all of them. A darker band of cells and a column of brighter cells sit in the middle of the lit region. Frames 4 to 6 add a caption, "2002 to 2007: 6 of 72 (8.3%)." In frames 5 and 6 the brighter column shifts slightly. A small block at the right edge looks like a marker or a house icon. Most of the left side is lit, and the right side is dark.

3. **What it means:** In most of the starting months on the left, buying came out ahead after ten years. The caption points to the 2002–2007 starting months as the exception. Only 6 of those 72 months, or 8.3%, favored the buyer. Those were the years when home prices peaked, and buyers who started then held through the crash. So the result depends on when you buy. Buying usually won, but not for every start date.

4. **Advice a viewer might take:** The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer could infer that buying has usually beaten renting over a ten-year hold, and that buying near a market peak can erase that advantage. The chart doesn't show a recommendation, and it says outright that it is not a forecast.

5. **Source of the conclusion:** The advice in 4 is my own inference. The on-screen text only says "history, not a forecast" and gives the 6 of 72 figure. It never tells the viewer to buy or to rent.
